t.E249.agn: In 2017 EFSA set the acceptable daily intake (ADI) at 0.07 mg/kg body weight, expressed as nitrite ion; intake in the general population remained below this limit, while a slight exceedance was seen in the highest-consuming children. Nitrite may form nitrosamines with certain substances in meat; IARC classifies ingested nitrite and nitrate under conditions that result in nitrosamine formation in Group 2A (probably carcinogenic to humans).
t.E249.body: Nitrite is almost completely absorbed from the intestine. Almost all of it is converted to nitrate in the body and excreted in the urine; the amount excreted in the urine as nitrite is about 0.02% of the dose. The main source of nitrite in the body is the conversion, by bacteria in the mouth, of nitrate taken in with food and water into nitrite.
t.E249.eff.0.t: In high amounts it may cause an increase in methaemoglobin, which reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen; EFSA's daily limit is based on this effect
t.E249.eff.1.t: It may form nitrosamines with certain substances in meat; IARC classifies ingested nitrite and nitrate under conditions that result in nitrosamine formation in Group 2A (probably carcinogenic to humans)
t.E249.eff.2.t: The daily limit may be slightly exceeded
t.E249.eval: IARC classifies the intake of nitrite and nitrate under conditions that may lead to nitrosamine formation in the body as Group 2A (probably carcinogenic). It is used in processed meats such as sucuk, sausages and salami to preserve colour and prevent botulism.
t.E249.prod: Produced chemically by the reduction of potassium nitrate.
t.E249.pw.0: According to EFSA, the daily limit may be slightly exceeded in the highest-consuming children.
t.E249.regx.0: Re-evaluated; ADI 0.07 mg/kg (expressed as nitrite ion).
t.E249.summary: A nitrite salt. In processed meats it preserves the pink colour and prevents the growth of the botulism bacterium.
t.E249.what: In processed meats it prevents the growth of the bacterium that causes botulism and preserves the pink colour.
